{{Short description|Pairs of sequences}}
: ''For complementary sequences in biology, see [[complementarity (molecular biology)]]. For integer sequences with complementary sets of members see [[Lambek–Moser theorem]].''
In applied mathematics, '''complementary sequences''' ('''CS''') are pairs of [[sequence]]s with the useful property that their out-of-phase aperiodic [[autocorrelation]] coefficients sum to zero. Binary complementary sequences were first introduced by [[Marcel J. E. Golay]] in 1949. In 1961–1962 Golay gave several methods for constructing sequences of length 2<sup>''N''</sup> and gave examples of complementary sequences of lengths 10 and 26.  In 1974 R. J. Turyn gave a method for constructing sequences of length ''mn'' from sequences of lengths ''m'' and ''n'' which allows the construction of sequences of any length of the form 2<sup>''N''</sup>10<sup>''K''</sup>26<sup>''M''</sup>.

Later the theory of complementary sequences was generalized by other authors to polyphase complementary sequences, multilevel complementary sequences, and arbitrary complex complementary sequences. '''Complementary sets''' have also been considered; these can contain more than two sequences.

== Definition ==

Let (''a''<sub>0</sub>, ''a''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''a''<sub>''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sub>) and (''b''<sub>0</sub>, ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''b''<sub>''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sub>) be a pair of bipolar sequences, meaning that ''a''(''k'') and ''b''(''k'') have values +1 or &minus;1. Let the aperiodic [[autocorrelation function]] of the sequence '''x''' be defined by

:<math>R_\mathbf{x}(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{N-k-1} x_jx_{j+k}.\,</math>

Then the pair of sequences ''a'' and ''b'' is complementary if:

:<math>R_a(k) + R_b(k) = 2N,\, </math>

for ''k'' = 0, and 

:<math>R_a(k) + R_b(k) = 0,\, </math>

for ''k'' = 1, ..., ''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1.

Or using [[Kronecker delta]] we can write:

:<math>R_a(k) + R_b(k) = 2N\delta(k),\, </math>

So we can say that the sum of autocorrelation functions of complementary sequences is a delta function, which is an ideal autocorrelation for many applications like [[radar]] [[pulse compression]] and [[spread spectrum]] [[telecommunications]].

== Examples ==

* As the simplest example we have sequences of length 2: (+1,&nbsp;+1) and (+1,&nbsp;&minus;1). Their autocorrelation functions are (2,&nbsp;1) and (2,&nbsp;&minus;1), which add up to (4,&nbsp;0).
* As the next example (sequences of length 4), we have (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1) and (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1). Their autocorrelation functions are (4,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;1) and (4,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1), which add up to (8,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;0).
* One example of length 8 is (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1) and (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1). Their autocorrelation functions are (8,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;3,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1) and (8,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;3,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;1).
* An example of length 10 given by Golay is (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1) and (+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;+1,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;&minus;1). Their autocorrelation functions are (10,&nbsp;&minus;3,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1,&minus;2,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;1) and (10,&nbsp;3,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;0,&nbsp;&minus;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;1,&nbsp;&minus;2,&nbsp;&minus;1).

== Properties of complementary pairs of sequences ==

* Complementary [[sequences]] have complementary spectra. As the autocorrelation function and the power spectra form a Fourier pair, complementary sequences also have complementary spectra. But as the Fourier transform of a delta function is a constant, we can write

:: <math>S_a + S_b = C_S,</math>

: where ''C''<sub>''S''</sub> is a constant.

: ''S''<sub>''a''</sub> and ''S''<sub>''b''</sub> are defined as a squared magnitude of the [[Fourier transform]] of the sequences. The Fourier transform can be a direct DFT of the sequences, it can be a DFT of zero padded sequences or it can be a continuous Fourier transform of the sequences which is equivalent to the [[Z transform]] for {{math|1=''Z'' = ''e''<sup>''j''ω</sup>}}.

* CS spectra is upper bounded. As ''S''<sub>''a''</sub> and ''S''<sub>''b''</sub> are non-negative values we can write

:: <math>S_a = C_S - S_b < C_S,</math>

: also

:: <math>S_b < C_S.</math>

* If either of the sequences of the CS pair is inverted (multiplied by −1) they remain complementary. More generally if any of the sequences is multiplied by ''e''<sup>''j''φ</sup> they remain complementary;
* If either of the sequences is reversed they remain complementary;
* If either of the sequences is delayed they remain complementary;
* If the sequences are interchanged they remain complementary;
* If both sequences are multiplied by the same constant (real or complex) they remain complementary;
* If alternating bits of both sequences are inverted they remain complementary. In general for arbitrary complex sequences if both sequences are multiplied by ''e''<sup>''j''&pi;''kn''/''N''</sup> (where ''k'' is a constant and ''n'' is the time index) they remain complementary;
* A new pair of complementary sequences can be formed as [''a'' ''b''] and [''a''&nbsp;−''b''] where [..] denotes concatenation and ''a'' and ''b'' are a pair of CS;
* A new pair of sequences can be formed as {''a'' ''b''} and {''a''&nbsp;−''b''} where {..} denotes [[Interleave sequence|interleaving]] of sequences.
* A new pair of sequences can be formed as ''a''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''b'' and ''a''&nbsp;−&nbsp;''b''.

==Golay pair==
A complementary pair ''a'', ''b'' may be encoded as polynomials ''A''(''z'') = ''a''(0) + ''a''(1)''z'' + ... + ''a''(''N''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)''z''<sup>''N''&minus;1</sup> and similarly for ''B''(''z'').  The complementarity property of the sequences is equivalent to the condition

:<math>\vert A(z) \vert^2 + \vert B(z) \vert^2 = 2N \, </math>

for all ''z'' on the unit circle, that is, |''z''|&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.  If so, ''A'' and ''B'' form a '''Golay pair''' of polynomials.  Examples include the [[Shapiro polynomials]], which give rise to complementary sequences of length a [[power of two]].

== Applications of complementary sequences ==

* Multislit spectrometry
* Ultrasound measurements
* Acoustic measurements
* [[radar]] [[pulse compression]]
* [[Wi-Fi]] networks, 
* [[3G]] [[CDMA]] wireless networks
* [[OFDM]] communication systems
* Train wheel detection systems<ref>
Donato, P.G.; Ureña, J.; Mazo, M.; Alvarez, F.
"Train wheel detection without electronic equipment near the rail line".
2004.
{{doi | 10.1109/IVS.2004.1336500 }}
</ref><ref>
J.J. Garcia; A. Hernandez; J. Ureña; J.C. Garcia; M. Mazo; J.L. Lazaro; M.C. Perez; F. Alvarez.
[http://geintra-uah.org/system/files/private/IV04_I.pdf "Low cost obstacle detection for smart railway infrastructures"].
2004.
</ref>
* Non-destructive tests (NDT)
* Communications
* [[coded aperture]] masks are designed using a 2-dimensional generalization of complementary sequences.
